source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

coverage.assignment: VI.C(2)(e–f) § 701(a)(2), Heckler v. Chaney, agency inaction/delay, Norton v. SUWA
coverage.notes: Two full assigned judicial opinions excerpted; other cases in textbook notes summarized as secondary authorities

topics.title: § 10.5 — Committed to Agency Discretion; Heckler v. Chaney (pp. 698–704)
topics.description: APA § 701(a)(2), meaning of 'no law to apply', default review of affirmative acts, exception for enforcement refusals.

entries.title: § 701(a)(1) versus § 701(a)(2)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: § 701(a)(1) requires Congress's preclusion of review by statute; § 701(a)(2) exempts action committed to agency discretion where there is no meaningful law or standard to apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: One doctrine asks whether Congress shut the courthouse; the other asks whether court has a standard for judging the agency's choice.
entries.legalExplanation: § 706(2)(A) separately permits abuse-of-discretion review when there are judicially manageable constraints. The § 701(a)(2) exception avoids contradiction for areas with genuinely unbounded choice.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish explicit/implied statutory exclusion from rare no-law-to-apply cases.
entries.examTrap: 'Discretion' does not automatically mean no judicial review: agencies often exercise reviewable discretion.

entries.title: § 701(a)(2) generally a very narrow exception for affirmative action
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Judicial review presumptively applies to agency approvals or affirmative actions where statutes supply standards; e.g. Overton Park's no feasible park alternative rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency saying 'yes' to a regulated project is often reviewable because judges can ask if statutory conditions were met.
entries.legalExplanation: Heckler cites Overton Park's language that § 701(a)(2) governs rare circumstances when statute is too broad to yield a meaningful review rule.
entries.examApplication: Find statutory commands like 'shall not approve' absent particular findings.
entries.examTrap: Do not mistake broad administrative discretion for absolute lawlessness.

entries.title: Heckler v. Chaney, 470 U.S. 821 (1985)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Ordinarily no. Agency non-enforcement decisions are presumptively committed to agency discretion and unreviewable, unless substantive law meaningfully constrains that choice; FDA refusal here not subject to APA judicial review.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency's refusal to commence investigative or enforcement action enjoys a rebuttable presumption of nonreviewability under § 701(a)(2), even though affirmative agency action generally is reviewable.
entries.legalExplanation: Deciding whether to enforce involves priorities, scarce resources, probability of success, practical enforcement value and agency expertise. Non-enforcement normally imposes no new coercive deprivation on private person and resembles prosecutor's discretion under Take Care Clause. Presumption can be rebutted by statutory guidelines such as Dunlop, while majority reserves other scenarios including blanket statutory abdication and some constitutional claims.
entries.examApplication: First classify decision as individual enforcement refusal versus general policy, rulemaking petition or affirmative act. Then look for specific statutory or regulatory mandates, constitutional claims or potential abdication.
entries.examTrap: Do not characterize Chaney as a total exemption for all agency inaction; the Court explicitly left possible exceptions and distinguished rulemaking denials.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt included in assigned uploaded chapter
entries.facts: Texas death-row inmate Chaney petitioned FDA to enforce Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act against drugs administered for lethal injections, alleging unapproved use and unsafe administration. FDA rejected enforcement on statutory and discretionary/resource grounds. Court of appeals found review possible; Supreme Court reversed.
entries.issue: Under APA § 701(a)(2), may a court review FDA decision refusing to investigate/prosecute third parties for alleged violation of an otherwise enforceable statute?
entries.holding: Ordinarily no. Agency non-enforcement decisions are presumptively committed to agency discretion and unreviewable, unless substantive law meaningfully constrains that choice; FDA refusal here not subject to APA judicial review.
entries.reasoning: Deciding whether to enforce involves priorities, scarce resources, probability of success, practical enforcement value and agency expertise. Non-enforcement normally imposes no new coercive deprivation on private person and resembles prosecutor's discretion under Take Care Clause. Presumption can be rebutted by statutory guidelines such as Dunlop, while majority reserves other scenarios including blanket statutory abdication and some constitutional claims.
entries.rule: Agency's refusal to commence investigative or enforcement action enjoys a rebuttable presumption of nonreviewability under § 701(a)(2), even though affirmative agency action generally is reviewable.

entries.title: Why Chaney presumes no review for enforcement refusals
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Enforcement triage depends on finite personnel/budget, case strength, alternative priorities, public impact, and Executive Branch charging discretion; no individual coercive action normally occurs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts aren't well placed to decide which alleged violator an agency should investigate next.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts ordinarily can review a completed enforcement sanction for statutory compliance; refusal lacks similarly focused coercive act.
entries.examApplication: Name specific institutional reasons, not merely cite administrative convenience.
entries.examTrap: One possible wrong legal interpretation in a refusal doesn't automatically make review available in every circuit.

entries.title: Rebutting non-enforcement presumption with mandatory statute
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Statute may impose enforcement duty or priorities; Dunlop required secretary to sue when a predicate finding (probable cause of union election violation) was made.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress can turn a normally optional lawsuit into mandatory duty when its specified conditions occur.
entries.legalExplanation: Heckler distinguishes permissive FDCA investigative provision from a 'shall sue if probable cause' provision.
entries.examApplication: Pinpoint words 'shall', threshold conditions, and whether agency has already determined statutory prerequisite.
entries.examTrap: A broad declaration of agency goals may not suffice to rebut Chaney.

entries.title: Dunlop v. Bachowski, 421 U.S. 560 (1975)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Congress gave reviewable mandatory enforcement trigger: Secretary of Labor shall sue to set aside a union election after finding probable cause of violation.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency cannot ignore a legally specified trigger for enforcement.
entries.legalExplanation: Illustrates substantive statute displacing general Chaney deference.
entries.examApplication: Contrast FDCA's 'authorized to investigate'.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Reserved Chaney scenarios: categorical abdication, jurisdiction, rights
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Majority reserved whether judicial review might exist where agency denies jurisdiction, adopts extreme general policy abandoning duties, or infringes constitutional rights.
entries.laymanExplanation: One refusal to prosecute is different from announcing a policy to never enforce a whole statute.
entries.legalExplanation: Possible challenges to broad legal interpretation documented in generally applicable policy may differ from individualized no-enforcement choices.
entries.examApplication: Describe potential theory as reserved/open; show textual or constitutional constraints.
entries.examTrap: Do not present every reserved exception as automatically established holding.

entries.title: Justice Marshall's concurrence: reviewable but deferential
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Justice Marshall would start from ordinary reviewability presumption and uphold FDA on the merits of broad enforcement discretion rather than find category nonreviewable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Marshall saw 'can court review?' as different from 'would challenge win?'
entries.legalExplanation: This is concurring opinion not majority law; it disputes new presumption but agrees with result.

topics.title: § 10.5 — Exceptions, Policy-based Nonenforcement and Other Discretion (pp. 704–710)
topics.description: Regents rescission, Weyerhaeuser, Mach Mining, rulemaking refusals, common-law prudential limits, state variations and FmHA foreclosure problem.

entries.title: DACA rescission reviewable: Regents distinct from simple non-enforcement
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: A broad program granting affirmative deferred-action status, work eligibility and benefits, and its rescission, is reviewable even if program relates to enforcement priorities.
entries.laymanExplanation: Removing DACA benefits was more than passively deciding not to prosecute certain people.
entries.legalExplanation: DHS v Regents held DACA creation and rescission produced affirmative immigration relief and structured interests; the rescission had concrete reviewable focus.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether decision simply defers enforcement or grants/withdraws benefits/eligibility of defined class.
entries.examTrap: Casebook's later discussion about litigation status is historically dated; do not claim current 2026 status based on it.

entries.title: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court held rescission of DACA reviewable: DACA conferred affirmative immigration relief and eligibility beyond bare nonprosecution.
entries.laymanExplanation: When government withdraws an affirmative program, courts can check how it did so.
entries.legalExplanation: The case is noted here for reviewability; fuller reasoned-decision discussion is in Chapter 9.
entries.examApplication: Differentiate rescission of program from individual Chaney refusal.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: § 701(a)(2) turns on meaningful standards and contextual prudence
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Review is available when statute/regulations contain judicially manageable guidelines; courts also consider traditional institutional boundaries, type of agency decision, public importance and discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: A broad term doesn't always mean nothing to review; some issues are traditionally left to administrators.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook contrasts Weyerhaeuser's required economic-benefit balancing, Webster's CIA national security discretion, and Department of Commerce's census review despite broad wording.
entries.examApplication: Search entire statutory framework and legally binding regulations for law to apply.
entries.examTrap: Treat 'no law to apply' as doctrinal starting point, but actual case outcomes may reflect additional prudential concerns.

entries.title: Weyerhaeuser Co. v. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 586 U.S. 9 (2018)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Reviewable critical-habitat exclusion decision where statute required comparison of conservation benefits against economic costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: A required balancing test gives judge law to apply, even when decision ultimately flexible.
entries.legalExplanation: Landowners alleged $34 million consequences for gopher frog habitat designation.
entries.examApplication: Compare bare 'may' language with substantive balancing criteria.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Webster v. Doe, 486 U.S. 592 (1988)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: CIA director's employee dismissal for national-interest reasons unreviewable on merits under § 701(a)(2), but constitutional claims remained.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts hesitate to second-guess spies' staffing decisions under broad discretionary statute.
entries.legalExplanation: Scalia dissent argued historical common-law limits broader than 'no law to apply'.
entries.examApplication: Separate regular merits from constitutional review.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Department of Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752 (2019)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Review permitted over citizenship question on census despite broad secretary authority to choose form and content.
entries.laymanExplanation: Accuracy and representational interests gave a meaningful legal benchmark.
entries.legalExplanation: Book sees concern about politically manipulative census as affecting choice to review.
entries.examApplication: Not all broad permissive wording is insulated.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: § 701(a)(2) is not identical to no explicit judicial metric
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Broader policy reasons sometimes support commitment to discretion (national intelligence, lump sum appropriations, reconsideration), while public constitutional/statutory concerns can justify review of apparently broad discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Historical function and public accountability can matter, not just how many 'shall's a statute contains.
entries.legalExplanation: Text notes Lincoln v Vigil nonrenewal of health program funding, ICC v BLE refusal to reopen, Dalton presidential base closing, and Census citizenship question.
entries.examApplication: Consider whole program, expected judicial role and availability of manageable constraints.
entries.examTrap: Do not turn these examples into universal exceptions without analyzing statute.

entries.title: Review of EEOC conciliation in Mach Mining is very limited
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Court may verify EEOC told employer about specific allegations and tried to discuss voluntary resolution, but may not judicially assess whether negotiations were in good faith.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge can check that required meeting attempt happened, not grade how hard EEOC bargained.
entries.legalExplanation: Title VII confidentiality and goal of stopping discrimination counsel narrow review; dispute distinguishable from labor collective bargaining good-faith scrutiny.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether required minimum communicative steps occurred and stop there.
entries.examTrap: Reviewable does not equal intrusive merits review.

entries.title: Mach Mining, LLC v. EEOC, 575 U.S. 480 (2015)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency conciliation duty reviewable for minimal effort to inform and discuss, not full good-faith bargaining.
entries.laymanExplanation: A narrow procedural standard can be judicially manageable.
entries.legalExplanation: Keeps confidentiality and avoids obstructing EEOC enforcement.
entries.examApplication: Contrast Chaney.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Rulemaking petition denial vs enforcement refusal
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Rulemaking denials are ordinarily judicially reviewable (extremely deferentially), because formal petitions produce stated reasons and legal issues; enforcement refusals generally presumed unreviewable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government saying 'we won't write a rule' normally can be checked more easily than 'we won't prosecute that violator'.
entries.legalExplanation: Massachusetts v EPA distinguished the categories but Conservancy of Southwest Florida found no law to apply to permissive critical habitat rulemaking petition.
entries.examApplication: Classify whether request is to enforce existing law or adopt new regulation; read mandatory vs permissive trigger.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply Chaney automatically to rulemaking petitions or assume every rulemaking denial reviewable.

entries.title: Massachusetts v. EPA, 549 U.S. 497 (2007)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency refusal to make greenhouse-gas rule judicially reviewable under Clean Air Act directions, although highly deferential on priorities.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency's statutory reasons for saying no can be reviewed.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast Conservancy's 'may' and lack of constraint on whether rulemaking should begin.
entries.examApplication: Tie to § 6.3 earlier notes.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Conservancy of Southwest Florida v. FWS, 677 F.3d 1073 (11th Cir. 2012)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Rulemaking petition denial unreviewable where statute 'may' designate habitat and contained no guiding standard.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some discretionary rulemaking choices are beyond meaningful review.
entries.legalExplanation: Scarce resources and permissive language made judicial review unworkable.
entries.examApplication: Compare Massachusetts.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Possible routes around Chaney without solving claim
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Potential arguments: specific statutory/regulatory mandate, agency's complete abdication, broadly applicable legal policy instead of individualized decision, private suit against violator, rulemaking petition or political action.
entries.laymanExplanation: When agency won't prosecute, look for other lawful approaches rather than treating every refusal as reviewable.
entries.legalExplanation: Crowley Caribbean distinguishes single refusal from broad general policy; courts vary; no assumption all alternatives succeed.
entries.examApplication: Construct alternative cause/claim and threshold before merits.
entries.examTrap: Do not invent a private right of action when statute has not provided one.

entries.title: State discretion cases vary even without federal-style § 701(a)(2)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Illinois Hanrahan excluded parole denial from review due to subjective predictive nature; Greer allowed review of housing financing despite 'sole judgment' phrase due to statutory income-mix standard.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state court may review a supposedly broad discretionary financing decision, yet decline prisoner parole review.
entries.legalExplanation: State statutes, policy and judicial workload affect reviewability; don't mechanically transfer federal tests.
entries.examApplication: Name jurisdiction and standards especially where state APA lacks § 701(a)(2) analogue.

topics.title: § 10.6 — Agency Inaction: Norton v. SUWA (pp. 710–715)
topics.description: § 706(1) review of agency omissions limited to discrete, legally required acts; distinguish broad land-use priorities and binding plans.

entries.title: APA §§ 551(13), 555(b) and 706(1): agency failure to act
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: APA defines agency action to include failure to act and permits compelling action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed, but SUWA restricts compelled action to discrete legally required acts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts may force agencies to do certain specific mandatory tasks, not generally manage entire programs.
entries.legalExplanation: § 551(13)'s rule/order/license/sanction/relief enumeration suggests discreteness; § 706(1) carries mandamus tradition and limits compelled action to duties law requires.
entries.examApplication: Ask two separate questions: is the requested act discrete? Is it legally required?
entries.examTrap: An agency's broadly stated mission to protect habitat is not itself a specific compellable action.

entries.title: Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 542 U.S. 55 (2004)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: No. Judicially enforceable failure to act requires an identifiable discrete agency action legally required. Broad nonimpairment mandate left BLM discretion over means, and general plan 'will monitor and close if warranted' statements weren't binding discrete commands. Supreme Court reversed the Tenth Circuit.
entries.laymanExplanation: APA § 706(1) authorizes compelling only a discrete legally required agency action; courts may require a mandated decision, not prescribe its discretionary outcome or supervise overall statutory performance.
entries.legalExplanation: § 551(13) treats failure to act as omission of discrete agency actions and ejusdem generis supports this. Historical mandamus only compelled clear nondiscretionary duty or required decision without dictating substance. Broad programmatic decree would thrust judges into daily resource allocation. Land plans often guide priorities, not create binding promises absent specific enforceable terms.
entries.examApplication: Identify alleged action (ban ORVs? conduct certain mandatory monitoring? issue a time-bound rule?), show exact statute/rule commands act, and separate general stewardship goals from specific performance duties.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse an agency's 'shall manage' objective with mandate to choose one named management technique, or assume every 'will do' plan is binding.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt included in assigned uploaded chapter
entries.facts: Environmental group SUWA sued federal Bureau of Land Management, alleging inadequate off-road-vehicle controls damaging wilderness study areas and inadequate implementation of commitments in BLM land-use plans. It requested court intervention to make BLM better manage use and implement monitoring.
entries.issue: May courts under APA § 706(1) compel broad agency compliance with environmental stewardship mandates or general land-use-plan intentions?
entries.holding: No. Judicially enforceable failure to act requires an identifiable discrete agency action legally required. Broad nonimpairment mandate left BLM discretion over means, and general plan 'will monitor and close if warranted' statements weren't binding discrete commands. Supreme Court reversed the Tenth Circuit.
entries.reasoning: § 551(13) treats failure to act as omission of discrete agency actions and ejusdem generis supports this. Historical mandamus only compelled clear nondiscretionary duty or required decision without dictating substance. Broad programmatic decree would thrust judges into daily resource allocation. Land plans often guide priorities, not create binding promises absent specific enforceable terms.
entries.rule: APA § 706(1) authorizes compelling only a discrete legally required agency action; courts may require a mandated decision, not prescribe its discretionary outcome or supervise overall statutory performance.

entries.title: SUWA element 1: discrete action
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Claim must target identifiable agency action comparable to rule, order, license, sanction or relief, not a generalized failure to run program effectively.
entries.laymanExplanation: A court can order a specific missing decision but can't just command an agency to fix an entire national program.
entries.legalExplanation: Ejusdem generis reading of APA § 551(13) precludes broad programmatic challenges of Lujan type.
entries.examApplication: Define exact omitted act in one sentence before testing legal mandate.
entries.examTrap: A vague plea to 'follow federal law' usually fails discreteness.

entries.title: SUWA element 2: legally required, not just desirable
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Act must be mandated by law or binding agency regulation; when manner is discretionary, court may compel occurrence but not direct substantive result.
entries.laymanExplanation: A mandatory deadline is enforceable, but judge cannot demand agency choose the petitioner's preferred policy.
entries.legalExplanation: Law may require an agency to act on application without specifying decision; § 706(1) allows ordering an answer, not dictating yes/no.
entries.examApplication: Identify mandatory verbs and precise duty, not just regulatory values.
entries.examTrap: A general plan statement about intended future use is not automatically legally required action.

entries.title: Land use plans normally guide agency priorities, not bind every promised step
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: General resource plans adopted after comment usually project priorities subject to funds, conditions and competing land uses; they may be binding only when source of independent or unmistakable duty.
entries.laymanExplanation: A five-year plan saying 'we'll monitor if warranted' often isn't an enforceable contract with courts.
entries.legalExplanation: SUWA left possibility that a plan reiterates existing legal mandate or expressly creates binding commitment. Otherwise broad judicial management distorts resource priorities.
entries.examApplication: Look at precision, mandatory versus conditional wording and external statute.
entries.examTrap: Not every written plan is meaningless; specific independent statutory obligations remain enforceable.

entries.title: Difference between failure to act and denial
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Failure to act is omission without final refusal; denial is agency saying no to a discrete request. Denial may get separate judicial-review and finality treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency ghosting a petition differs from issuing a negative final answer.
entries.legalExplanation: SUWA reads § 551(13) to require discreteness for both; Massachusetts v EPA addressed denial of rulemaking petition.
entries.examApplication: Identify whether case seeks review of refusal or compulsion after delay.
entries.examTrap: Don't label a general policy disagreement as a discrete omitted decision.

topics.title: § 10.6 Notes — Unreasonable Agency Delay and TRAC (pp. 715–719)
topics.description: Time to act, statutory deadlines, TRAC six factors, Heckler v Day, Community Voice, mandatory study and Gloria hypothetical.

entries.title: APA § 555(b) reasonable-time requirement
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Within reasonable time, agency shall proceed to conclude matter presented; § 706(1) may compel action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed where underlying action is legally required.
entries.laymanExplanation: When an agency owes you a decision, endless silence may be challengeable even without fixed statutory deadline.
entries.legalExplanation: SUWA's mandatory-discrete limitation still governs type of action. § 555(b) can provide timing obligation for lawfully presented matters, but no automatic right to preferred merits outcome.
entries.examApplication: Identify specific unresolved matter, underlying duty to conclude, duration and statutory timetable.
entries.examTrap: § 555(b) is not blanket license to sue any agency whenever it has not implemented aspirational goals.

entries.title: Six TRAC factors for unreasonable delay
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: TRAC evaluates: (1) rule of reason; (2) congressional timetable; (3) heightened importance of health/welfare; (4) effect of accelerating one matter on competing priorities; (5) prejudice to affected persons; (6) no need to prove impropriety.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judges ask how long and why, whether people are suffering, and what government work would be displaced if this case jumps the line.
entries.legalExplanation: Telecommunications Research & Action Center v. FCC (D.C. Cir. 1984) sets six non-mechanical considerations for mandamus-like agency-delay relief.
entries.examApplication: Apply all six to given timelines, statutory deadlines, health harms and agency resource allocation; explain likely limited remedy.
entries.examTrap: A plaintiff does not have to prove bad faith; time alone never resolves all factors.

entries.title: TRAC v. FCC, 750 F.2d 70 (D.C. Cir. 1984)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Delay resolving AT&T overcharge dispute was concerning but FCC had made commitments and schedules; court retained jurisdiction rather than command immediate outcome.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court can monitor rather than dictate agency merits.
entries.legalExplanation: Court balanced six factors including priorities and public impact.
entries.examApplication: For remedies, distinguish order compelling deadline and retained jurisdiction.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Courts wary of reallocating national agency resources
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Ordering instant action in one region may postpone action elsewhere and undermine Congress's chosen decision quality; courts weigh systemwide effects.
entries.laymanExplanation: Speeding one case can slow hundreds of others.
entries.legalExplanation: Heckler v Day reversed classwide fixed Social Security disability hearing deadlines in Vermont because Congress had rejected mandatory timelines and other states would bear transferred burden.
entries.examApplication: Analyze competing public welfare, resource limits and whether statute directs priority.
entries.examTrap: Never assume 'agency is busy' defeats explicit legal commands automatically.

entries.title: Heckler v. Day, 467 U.S. 104 (1984)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court disapproved judicially imposed 90-day Social Security administrative disability hearing deadline contrary to congressional treatment of timetables.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts shouldn't casually force rushed decisions or interstate resource reshuffling.
entries.legalExplanation: Consider § 555(b) and actual congressional timetable choices.
entries.examApplication: Contrast Community Voice health emergency.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: In re A Community Voice, 878 F.3d 779 (9th Cir. 2019)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Eight years after EPA granted petition to update lead-dust protections, it still had no proposed rule and speculative dates years in future; court found unreasonable delay, highlighting childhood lead exposure.
entries.laymanExplanation: Children's health and years of inactivity outweighed mere assurances of later consideration.
entries.legalExplanation: Dissent said rulemaking need not be mandatory after granting petition and agency had recently completed science.
entries.examApplication: TRAC factor (3) health and (1) length important, with priority arguments on both sides.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook Notes and Questions; full opinion not excerpted

entries.title: TRAC analysis requires discretion and remedy separation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: Even when unreasonable delay found, a court may compel timely completion, request timetable, or retain jurisdiction rather than dictate specific regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judicial oversight can set clock without writing agency policy.
entries.legalExplanation: SUWA restricts mandated agency act, while TRAC weighs whether failure to complete it is unreasonable; remedy should preserve substantive agency discretion.
entries.examApplication: First find required discrete act; next delay; finally craft narrow order.
entries.examTrap: Failure to make progress is not itself proof court may prescribe final outcome.

entries.title: Mandatory local study as a potentially discrete act
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.summary: A city ordinance specifically requiring a planning department to conduct a gentrification impact/mitigation study is more specific than broad mission directives, but remedy still turns on duty wording, timing and procedural prerequisites.
entries.laymanExplanation: A city council command to do one defined study is unlike a vague promise to improve neighborhoods.
entries.legalExplanation: Apply SUWA's discreteness/legal-duty test, § 555(b), TRAC and source state law; professor's hypothetical assumes standing and federal-style admin law.
entries.examApplication: Don't solve merely because mayor disagrees with council or plaintiff lacks money; analyze all thresholds.

problems.title: Chaney: review of refusal to enforce
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 703–704)
problems.prompt: List distinct reasons nonenforcement is presumptively unreviewable, then test whether a specific statute, general abdication policy or constitutional claim changes result without resolving new facts.

problems.title: Benzene nondelegation versus Chaney discretion
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 704)
problems.prompt: How can Chief Justice Rehnquist's skepticism of unlimited agency legislative discretion in Benzene coexist with broad enforcement-discretion shield in Chaney? Distinguish policy making versus prosecution.

problems.title: Farmers Home Administration / Mary's drought foreclosure — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 709–710)
problems.prompt: FmHA § 19 provides Secretary 'may' grant deferral/forgo foreclosure upon borrower request when circumstances beyond control create temporary inability to pay without impairment of living. Drought ruined Mary's crop; agency never notified borrowers and has never used relief because viewed it as optional; it foreclosed without Mary requesting relief. Should court affirm foreclosure? What relief if any? Does analysis change if Mary made timely request but FmHA denied? Consider law to apply, mandatory predicates, discretion, procedural duty and remedy, but leave unanswered.

problems.title: Regents versus Chaney
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 704–705)
problems.prompt: Why does conferral and withdrawal of deferred-action benefits qualify as affirmative reviewable agency action when isolated prosecution discretion is generally unreviewable?

problems.title: Law to apply: Weyerhaeuser, Webster and census
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 704–707)
problems.prompt: Contrast concrete cost/conservation balancing, CIA national security staffing, and census accuracy. Which contextual/statutory features make review appropriate?

problems.prompt: If EEOC conveyed allegations and made some discussion attempt, should court grade its demands as good faith? Identify court's limited inquiry and why.

problems.title: Rulemaking denials — Massachusetts versus Conservancy

problems.title: SUWA: nonimpairment mandate versus specific ORV ban
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 713–715)
problems.prompt: Would § 706(1) permit a court to order that BLM prohibit ORVs to meet statutory wilderness nonimpairment objective? Why may a court compel a statutory duty without choosing regulatory tools?

problems.title: When is a land-use promise binding?
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 714–715)
problems.prompt: Can a resource plan statement 'will monitor and close if warranted' support judicial compulsion? Would it differ if the plan repeats a precise mandatory statutory duty?

problems.title: Gloria / Kenwood gentrification study — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 719)
problems.prompt: City Council passed ordinance requiring Planning Department to study economic effects of gentrification and mitigation; Mayor Joe secretly directed indefinite deferral because rising tax revenues and crime declines appeal to him. Gloria, a Kenwood renter, faces displacement and lacks funds. Assume state law parallels federal administrative law and Gloria has standing. Evaluate whether court can order department to study, duty/timing/discreteness, possible remedy and fees, without answering.

problems.title: Apply all six TRAC factors
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 716–718)
problems.prompt: Agency received public health petition eight years ago, acknowledged harm, but gave only speculative future deadlines. Apply TRAC factors in detail, contrast competing higher agency priorities and predict remedies without supplying conclusion.

problems.title: SUWA + TRAC combined exam attack
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 710–719)
problems.prompt: A litigant asks court to compel one agency to improve all pollution inspections and separately to decide a mandatory specific permit by deadline. Test discrete legally required act, difference between discretion and time, TRAC reasonableness and scope of judicial order.

problems.title: Community Voice versus Heckler v Day
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 10, pp. 698–719 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 716–718)
problems.prompt: When can serious public health consequences justify intervention despite limited resources? What statutory deadlines or congressional decisions weigh the other way?
